source_title: Comparative efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitor class members in patients with heart failure and type 2 diabetes: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

entries.canonical_statement: The review evaluated class effects of SGLT2 inhibitors versus control and compared individual SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with both heart failure and type 2 diabetes.
The systematic review and network meta-analysis was reported according to the 2015 PRISMA-NMA guidance and was registered in PROSPERO as CRD42022366372, with no changes to the posted protocol.
The search covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, medRxiv, SSRN, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception through April 15, 2025.
Two authors independently screened studies and extracted data, with disagreements resolved by discussion with a third author.
Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2.0 and quality of evidence was graded per outcome with GRADE across risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias.

Pairwise meta-analysis used random effects with inverse-variance pooling, Paule-Mandel between-study variance, Hartung-Knapp confidence-interval adjustment when at least five RCTs were available, hazard ratios as the primary dichotomous effect measure, relative risks as secondary, and mean differences for continuous outcomes.

Pairwise heterogeneity was evaluated with I-squared, funnel plots and Egger testing were used when at least 10 RCTs were available, prespecified subgroup analyses included control type, ejection-fraction category, follow-up time, trial phase, prediabetes inclusion, and risk of bias, and a post hoc subgroup analysis used the study primary population.

Frequentist network meta-analysis compared individual SGLT2 inhibitors, placebo, and standard of care; transitivity was judged from patient characteristics, dose, control type, outcome definitions, and follow-up, consistency was tested, and interventions were ranked with p-scores from 0 to 1.
Analyses were performed in R version 4.3.1 using the meta package for pairwise meta-analysis and netmeta for network meta-analysis.
Stroke was a secondary outcome of the review.
Renal dysfunction was a secondary outcome of the review.
Acute kidney injury was a secondary outcome of the review.
Diabetic ketoacidosis was a secondary outcome of the review.
Hypotension was a secondary outcome of the review.
Hypoglycemia was a secondary outcome of the review.
Hyperkalemia was a secondary outcome of the review.
Bone fracture was a secondary outcome of the review.
Amputation was a secondary outcome of the review.
Urinary tract infection was a secondary outcome of the review.
Genital infection was a secondary outcome of the review.
Serious adverse events was a secondary outcome of the review.
Adverse events leading to discontinuation was a secondary outcome of the review.
Systolic blood pressure was a secondary outcome of the review.
Diastolic blood pressure was a secondary outcome of the review.
Weight was a secondary outcome of the review.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate was a secondary outcome of the review.
Edema was a secondary outcome of the review.
The search identified 3,201 records, 1,537 remained after deduplication, 120 full-text articles were assessed, and 75 articles representing 17 unique randomized controlled trials were included.
Across the 17 included randomized controlled trials, 17,809 participants had both heart failure and type 2 diabetes.
Nine included trials enrolled heart failure and type 2 diabetes as the main study population, while eight large trials supplied outcome data for the dual-diagnosis subgroup.
The evidence network included canagliflozin in 2 trials, dapagliflozin in 6, empagliflozin in 6, ertugliflozin in 1, ipragliflozin in 1, and sotagliflozin in 1.
Thirteen included trials used placebo and four used standard of care as the control.
In pairwise meta-analysis of SGLT2 inhibitors versus control, all-cause mortality had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.98; 9 RCTs; I² 26%; low quality of evidence).

In pairwise meta-analysis of SGLT2 inhibitors versus control, cardiovascular death had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.00; 10 RCTs; I² 23%; very low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis of SGLT2 inhibitors versus control, all-cause hospitalization had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.74 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.88; 2 RCTs; I² 0%; high quality of evidence).

In pairwise meta-analysis of SGLT2 inhibitors versus control, hospitalization for heart failure had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.77; 12 RCTs; I² 2%; source certainty labels are internally inconsistent across abstract/results/Table 2).
Table 2 reported a relative risk of 0.91 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.00) for all-cause mortality across 13,994 participants in 9 RCTs, with low GRADE certainty.
Table 2 reported a relative risk of 0.96 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.13) for cardiovascular death across 15,850 participants in 10 RCTs, with very low GRADE certainty.
Table 2 reported a relative risk of 0.80 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.84) for all-cause hospitalization across 1,507 participants in 2 RCTs, with high GRADE certainty.
Table 2 reported a relative risk of 0.73 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.78) for hospitalization for heart failure across 15,954 participants in 11 RCTs, with low GRADE certainty.
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, serious adverse events had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.86 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.91; 9 RCTs; I² 0%; moderate quality of evidence).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, hyperkalemia had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.82 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.91; 5 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, hypotension had a pooled hazard ratio of 1.17 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.34; 5 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, genital infection had a pooled hazard ratio of 3.14 (95% CI 1.86 to 5.28; 3 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, stroke had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.19; 3 RCTs; I² 0%; moderate quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, renal dysfunction had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.77 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; 7 RCTs; I² 29%; low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, diabetic ketoacidosis had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.63 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.68; 3 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, hypoglycemia had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.95 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.14; 7 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, bone fracture had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.98 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.33; 6 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).

In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, adverse events leading to discontinuation had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.07; 7 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, acute kidney injury had a pooled hazard ratio of 1.02 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.13; 5 RCTs; I² 0%; moderate quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, amputation had a pooled hazard ratio of 1.17 (95% CI 0.65 to 2.12; 6 RCTs; I² 44%; moderate quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, urinary tract infection had a pooled hazard ratio of 1.14 (95% CI 0.95 to 1.36; 3 RCTs; I² 0%; low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, the pooled mean difference for estimated glomerular filtration rate was 3.00 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 1.71 to 4.30; 7 RCTs; I² 15%; low quality of evidence).

In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, the pooled mean difference for diastolic blood pressure was -2.87 mmHg (95% CI -6.31 to 0.57; 5 RCTs; I² 63%; very low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).

In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, the pooled mean difference for systolic blood pressure was -1.94 mmHg (95% CI -5.81 to 1.93; 7 RCTs; I² 74%; very low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
In pairwise meta-analysis versus control, the pooled mean difference for weight was -0.90 kg (95% CI -2.02 to 0.22; 8 RCTs; I² 30%; very low quality of evidence; not statistically significant).
The effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on edema could not be determined because data were available from only one randomized trial.
In the network meta-analysis, no individual SGLT2 inhibitor significantly affected cardiovascular death.
Dapagliflozin was the only individual SGLT2 inhibitor that significantly reduced all-cause mortality versus placebo in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.98).
Canagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.81).
Dapagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87).
Empagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.82).
Ertugliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.94).
Sotagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.83).
Canagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus standard of care in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.21, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.53).
Dapagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus standard of care in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.70).
Empagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus standard of care in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.64).
Ertugliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus standard of care in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.64).
Sotagliflozin significantly reduced hospitalization for heart failure versus standard of care in the network meta-analysis (HR 0.24, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.59).
Canagliflozin was the highest-ranked treatment for all-cause mortality with a p-score of 0.86.
Canagliflozin was the highest-ranked treatment for cardiovascular death with a p-score of 0.82.
Canagliflozin was the highest-ranked treatment for hospitalization for heart failure with a p-score of 0.88.
In the Mixed ejection fraction subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for all-cause mortality was HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.93; interaction p=0.03).
In the HFrEF subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for all-cause mortality was HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.96; interaction p=0.03).
In the HFpEF subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for all-cause mortality was HR 0.98 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.09; interaction p=0.03; not statistically significant).
In the Mixed ejection fraction subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for renal dysfunction was HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.87; interaction p=0.03).
In the HFrEF subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for renal dysfunction was HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.91; interaction p=0.03).
In the HFpEF subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for renal dysfunction was HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.30; interaction p=0.03; not statistically significant).
In the Studies including prediabetes subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for hospitalization for heart failure was HR 0.15 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.64; 1 RCT; interaction p=0.04).
In the Studies not including prediabetes subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for hospitalization for heart failure was HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.77; 11 RCTs; interaction p=0.04).
In the Mixed ejection fraction subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for amputation was HR 2.46 (95% CI 1.21 to 4.99; interaction p=0.01).
In the T2DM primary population subgroup, the SGLT2 inhibitor class effect for amputation was HR 2.32 (95% CI 1.10 to 4.90; CANVAS Program only; interaction p=0.04).
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Dapagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of mean difference (mmHg) -8.15 (95% CI -13.01 to -3.29) for diastolic blood pressure.
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Empagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of mean difference (mmHg) -2.51 (95% CI -4.83 to -0.18) for diastolic blood pressure.
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Empagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of mean difference (mL/min/1.73 m²) 2.97 (95% CI 2.30 to 3.63) for estimated glomerular filtration rate.
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Empagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of hazard ratio 3.04 (95% CI 1.78 to 5.20) for genital infection.
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Canagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of hazard ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.97) for serious adverse events.
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Dapagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of hazard ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.95) for serious adverse events.
In the individual-drug network meta-analysis, Empagliflozin versus placebo had an effect of hazard ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.92) for serious adverse events.
Network meta-analysis provides lower certainty than head-to-head randomized comparisons because individual-drug contrasts are largely indirect.
Canagliflozin’s high ranking was derived from only two randomized trials containing 1,543 patients with the dual diagnosis, so the ranking requires caution.
The 17 included randomized trials enrolled 65,380 participants overall, but only 17,809 belonged to the heart-failure plus type-2-diabetes target population.
Limited data for MACE, lower-limb amputation, edema, heart-failure stage/type, and body mass index forced outcome modifications and restricted subgroup interpretation.
Three included randomized trials had high risk of bias and five had some concerns.

Potential heterogeneity arose from differing outcome definitions, baseline heart-failure severity, studies not designed for the dual-diagnosis subgroup, concomitant treatments, and different SGLT2 inhibitor doses.
GRADE certainty was primarily based on relative risks because absolute effects per arm could not be calculated from hazard ratios.

The source contains an internal certainty-label discrepancy for hospitalization for heart failure: the abstract and Table 2 label the evidence low certainty, while the Results prose describes moderate quality of evidence.

The main-text extracted wording for hypotension is inconsistent with the supplement: the supplement reports HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.34), which is internally coherent with a 17% increase and is used as the supported quantitative result.

Table 2 reports an eGFR mean difference in the direction of lower eGFR, whereas the supplementary Figure S33 and Secondary Results S1 report a significant +3.00 mL/min/1.73 m² increase; this discrepancy is unresolved in the supplied source package.

The article notes that some Summary-of-Findings relative-risk estimates differ from hazard-ratio forest plots because CANVAS Program supplied incidence rates without event counts, preventing relative-risk calculation for several outcomes.

The authors concluded that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce all-cause mortality, hospitalization for heart failure, and serious adverse events in patients with heart failure and type 2 diabetes, while increasing hypotension, eGFR, and genital infection relative to placebo or standard of care.

The authors concluded that canagliflozin ranked best for reducing all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, and hospitalization for heart failure, while calling for head-to-head comparisons in more homogeneous populations.
The authors reported that the review received no specific grant from public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agencies.
The authors declared no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work.
